scenes.heading: Profit, loss and discounts
scenes.sub: Is that deal as good as it looks?
scenes.say: Every business needs to know if it's making a profit or a loss. Every shopper wants to know how good a discount really is. Today you'll use multipliers to answer both.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Spend $20 on a lemonade stand, sell it all for $35
scenes.breaks: Real businesses also pay rent, wages and tax, so a real owner keeps less than this simple profit.
scenes.say: Imagine a lemonade stand. You spend twenty dollars on supplies: that's the cost price. You sell everything for thirty-five dollars: that's the selling price. You've made a fifteen dollar profit. As a percentage of what you spent, fifteen out of twenty is a seventy-five per cent profit.
scenes.caption: Imagine a lemonade stand. You spend $20 on supplies: the cost price. You sell everything for $35: the selling price. You've made a $15 profit. As a percentage of what you spent, 15 out of 20 is a 75% profit.

scenes.heading: Percentage profit
scenes.say: Profit is the selling price minus the cost price. If it's negative, that's a loss. To make it a percentage, always divide by the cost price, then multiply by one hundred per cent.

scenes.heading: A mark-up
scenes.question: A shop buys a hoodie for $35 and marks it up by 60%. Find the selling price and profit.
scenes.say: A shop buys a hoodie for thirty-five dollars and marks it up by sixty per cent. That's times one point six, so it sells for fifty-six dollars. The profit is twenty-one dollars.
scenes.caption: A shop buys a hoodie for $35 and marks it up by 60%. That's × 1.6, so it sells for $56. The profit is $21.

scenes.heading: A mark-up as a bar
scenes.say: The cost price is the one hundred per cent bar. The mark-up adds sixty per cent more, so the selling price is one hundred and sixty per cent of the cost.
scenes.caption: The cost price is 100%. The mark-up adds 60%, so the selling price is 160% of the cost.

scenes.heading: Discount, backwards
scenes.question: After a 30% discount, sneakers cost $129.50. What was the marked price?
scenes.say: After a thirty per cent discount, sneakers cost one hundred and twenty-nine dollars fifty. Thirty per cent off means you pay seventy per cent, so times zero point seven. To go backwards, divide by zero point seven. The marked price was one hundred and eighty-five dollars.
scenes.caption: After a 30% discount, sneakers cost $129.50. 30% off means you pay 70%, so × 0.7. To go backwards, divide by 0.7. The marked price was $185.

scenes.heading: Mark-up, then a sale
scenes.question: A lamp costs a shop $45. It's marked up 60%, then 25% off in a sale. Percentage profit?
scenes.say: A lamp costs a shop forty-five dollars. It's marked up sixty per cent to seventy-two dollars, then twenty-five per cent off in a sale gives fifty-four dollars. The profit is nine dollars, and nine out of forty-five is a twenty per cent profit. Not thirty-five per cent: the discount comes off the bigger price.
scenes.caption: A lamp costs a shop $45. Marked up 60% to $72, then 25% off gives $54. The profit is $9, and 9 out of 45 is a 20% profit. Not 35%: the discount comes off the bigger price.

scenes.heading: One step at a time
scenes.say: Follow the chain: forty-five dollars times one point six is seventy-two, then times zero point seven five is fifty-four.
scenes.caption: $45 × 1.6 = $72, then × 0.75 = $54.

scenes.heading: Watch out

left.title: Correct
points: Chains: one price at a time

scenes.say: Watch out. Percentage profit always divides by the cost price. To find an original price, divide by the multiplier. To remove GST, divide by one point one. And for a chain of changes, work out one price at a time.
scenes.caption: Watch out. Percentage profit always divides by the cost price. To find an original price, divide by the multiplier. To remove GST, ÷ 1.1. For a chain of changes, work out one price at a time.

scenes.say: Quick recap. Profit is selling price minus cost price. Percentage profit or loss divides by the cost price. Mark-ups multiply up and discounts multiply down. Work backwards by dividing. And GST adds ten per cent. Now try the practice questions!
